title: What does it mean that a Stream does not store elements (pipeline over a source, lazy, pull-based)?
shortTitle: Why do streams not store elements?

s1_definition.profdef: A Stream is a PIPELINE DESCRIPTION, not a data structure. It does not allocate memory to hold elements. When you call `list.stream().filter(...).map(...)`, Java builds a chain of operation descriptors (like a recipe) — no element is processed yet. When a terminal operation runs, it PULLS elements one-at-a-time from the source through the pipeline: the terminal asks the last intermediate for an element, that intermediate asks the one before it, and so on back to the source. This is PULL-BASED execution (consumer drives) as opposed to PUSH-BASED (producer drives). Benefits: (1) only processes what's needed (short-circuit: `findFirst` stops after first match), (2) handles infinite sources (`Stream.generate()`), (3) minimal memory — only ONE element is in-flight at a time (unless a stateful op like `sorted` buffers), (4) fusion — multiple operations on same element happen in one pass, not separate loops.
s1_definition.analogy: A Collection is like a bank safe with 10,000 cheques stored inside. A Stream is like the cheque-clearing CONVEYOR BELT — it stores ZERO cheques. Cheques enter from the source (vault), pass through verification (filter), get stamped (map), and reach the destination (terminal). The conveyor belt pulls ONE cheque at a time. If the destination says "I only need 5 cleared cheques" (limit/findFirst), the belt STOPS — the remaining 9,995 cheques are never pulled from the vault. No wasted work.
s1_definition.oneliner: Stream = pipeline description, not storage. Pull-based: terminal pulls one element at a time through the chain. Lazy: nothing happens until terminal. Minimal memory: one element in-flight (unless sorted/distinct).

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's fraud detection system scans 50 million daily transactions.** The old system loaded ALL transactions into a List, then looped 3 times: once to filter suspicious (amount > Rs.10 lakh), once to extract account details, once to find the first match for a specific pattern. With streams: one pull-based pipeline, elements processed one-at-a-time, stops at first match (findFirst). Memory: O(1) instead of O(n).

**What the project will show:** Pull-based execution with logging (proves one-at-a-time), fusion (single pass), short-circuit (findFirst stops early), infinite stream (alert ID generator), and stateful vs stateless memory comparison.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `findFirstSuspicious("SAV2001")` loads 5 transactions from DB into a List.

**Step 2.** `.stream()` wraps the list as a stream source. STORES NOTHING — just holds a reference to the list's iterator.

**Step 3.** `.filter(...)` and `.map(...)` add stages to the pipeline descriptor. NOTHING EXECUTES.

**Step 4.** `.findFirst()` triggers pull-based execution. It says: "give me one element."

**Step 5 — PULL #1.** Source yields TXN-001 (Rs.500, India). Filter checks: amount > 10L? NO. High-risk country? NO. → DROPPED. findFirst says: "give me another."

**Step 6 — PULL #2.** Source yields TXN-002 (Rs.15L, Nigeria). Filter checks: amount > 10L? YES → PASSES. Map creates SuspiciousTxn DTO. findFirst receives it → DONE! **Pipeline stops. TXN-004, TXN-006, TXN-007 are NEVER pulled from source.**

**Step 7.** Result: processed 2 of 5 elements. 60% of work saved by short-circuit.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ PULL-BASED EXECUTION — findFirst ═══

  Terminal: findFirst()
    │ "give me ONE element"
    ▼
  Stage: map(t → SuspiciousTxn)
    │ "give me ONE element"
    ▼
  Stage: filter(isSuspicious)
    │ "give me ONE element"
    ▼
  Source: List.iterator()
    │ yields TXN-001 (Rs.500, India)
    ▼
  filter: Rs.500 < 10L AND India not risky → DROP (Avoid) 
    │ "give me ANOTHER element"
    ▼
  Source: yields TXN-002 (Rs.15L, Nigeria)
    ▼
  filter: Rs.15L > 10L → PASS (Recommended) 
    ▼
  map: TXN-002 → SuspiciousTxn DTO
    ▼
  findFirst: received! → STOP (Recommended) 
    (TXN-004, TXN-006, TXN-007 NEVER PULLED!)

  ═══ FUSION — ONE PASS, NOT THREE ═══

  WITHOUT fusion (hypothetical — 3 passes):
    Pass 1: filter ALL 5 txns → [TXN-002, TXN-004, TXN-007]
    Pass 2: map ALL 3 → [DTO, DTO, DTO]
    Pass 3: collect ALL 3 → List

  WITH fusion (actual — 1 pass):
    TXN-001: filter(DROP) → next
    TXN-002: filter(PASS) → map(DTO) → collect → next
    TXN-004: filter(PASS) → map(DTO) → collect → next
    TXN-006: filter(DROP) → next
    TXN-007: filter(PASS) → map(DTO) → collect → DONE

    Each element goes through ALL ops before next element is pulled!

  ═══ STATELESS vs STATEFUL MEMORY ═══

  Stateless (filter, map, flatMap, peek):
    O(1) memory — ONE element in-flight
    Element enters → processed → exits → forgotten

  Stateful (sorted, distinct):
    O(n) memory — must BUFFER elements
    sorted: must see ALL before emitting any
    distinct: must track seen elements in HashSet

  ═══ STREAM STORES NOTHING — PROOF ═══

  Stream<T> has NO:
    .size()        ← doesn't know how many elements
    .get(index)    ← no random access
    .contains(x)   ← no membership check
    .add(x)        ← no mutation
    .iterator()    ← wait, it does... but single-use!
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Stream does not store elements — it is a pipeline description that processes elements on demand from a source. The execution is pull-based: the terminal operation drives the pipeline by requesting elements one at a time. The terminal asks the last intermediate stage for an element, which asks the previous stage, which asks the source. Each element flows through all stateless stages (filter, map) before the next element is pulled. This means only one element is in-flight at any time, requiring O(1) memory for stateless operations.

In my fraud scan service, findFirst demonstrates short-circuit pull-based execution. The pipeline has 5 transactions but only pulls 2: TXN-001 is pulled and dropped by the filter, TXN-002 is pulled, passes the filter, gets mapped to a DTO, and findFirst receives it and STOPS. The remaining 3 transactions are never pulled from the source — 60% of work saved. The logs prove element-by-element processing: pull, filter, map happen on ONE element before the next is requested.

This design enables three powerful capabilities. First, fusion: filter, map, and collect execute in a single pass over the data, not three separate loops. Second, short-circuit: findFirst, limit, and anyMatch stop the pipeline as soon as the result is determined. Third, infinite streams: Stream.generate and Stream.iterate produce elements forever, which works because the stream stores nothing — it just pulls elements until a limit or findFirst stops it. The exception is stateful operations like sorted and distinct, which must buffer elements internally — sorted needs all elements before it can sort, requiring O(n) memory.
